title: Accepting the Prussian Minister-Presidency
context: Prussia faced a constitutional conflict over army reform and budget authority.
decision: Accepted the minister-presidency and governed despite parliamentary opposition.
alternatives: Compromise immediately; refuse office; seek settlement first.
rationale_reconstruction: Preserve executive capacity and complete military reform before constitutional accommodation.
criticism: Deepened constitutional conflict and normalized strong executive government.
sources: Jonathan Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life | Encyclopaedia Britannica — Otto von Bismarck

title: Supporting Russia during the Polish January Uprising
context: A Polish uprising threatened Russia and could affect Prussia's eastern security.
rationale_reconstruction: Maintain neutrality; support Polish nationalists; seek mediation.
outcome: Prevent a hostile Polish mobilization and preserve Russian goodwill.
criticism: Prussia improved relations with Russia and reduced security risk on its eastern flank.
scale: Damaged liberal/nationalist legitimacy and was coercive toward Polish aspirations.
column20: Jonathan Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life | Bismarck diplomatic history

title: Using the Schleswig-Holstein crisis against Denmark
context: The Schleswig-Holstein question created a German-national conflict with Denmark.
decision: Cooperated with Austria in a limited war against Denmark.
alternatives: Act alone; avoid war; pursue an international settlement.
rationale_reconstruction: Create a bounded conflict that increases Prussian leverage while retaining Austria as a temporary partner.
outcome: Denmark was defeated; Schleswig and Holstein came under joint Prussian-Austrian administration.
criticism: The settlement preserved an unresolved issue with Austria.
sources: Jonathan Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life | Encyclopaedia Britannica — Schleswig-Holstein

title: Fighting Austria in the Seven Weeks' War
context: Prussia and Austria competed for leadership of the German states.
decision: Pushed the crisis to war and then sought limited peace after victory.
alternatives: Accept dual leadership; avoid war; destroy Austria as a power.
rationale_reconstruction: Exclude Austria from German affairs without destroying it as a future counterweight or partner.
outcome: Prussia won decisively; the North German Confederation followed.
criticism: War could have escalated or produced a worse coalition outcome.
sources: Jonathan Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life | Lothar Gall, Bismarck: The White Revolutionary

title: Building the North German Confederation
context: Victory over Austria created an opening for political reorganization of northern Germany.
decision: Established a federal structure dominated by Prussia.
alternatives: Centralized annexation; restore loose confederation; delay settlement.
rationale_reconstruction: Convert battlefield leverage into an institutional order acceptable to multiple German states.
outcome: Prussia's leadership became institutionalized across northern Germany.
criticism: Retained strong monarchical and Prussian dominance.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — North German Confederation | Jonathan Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life

title: Editing and publishing the Ems Dispatch
context: A diplomatic dispute over the Spanish succession and French demands produced a high-risk confrontation.
rationale_reconstruction: Suppress it; publish full text; continue private diplomacy.
outcome: Change political incentives so war appears more defensible for Prussia.
criticism: France declared war; German states rallied; war accelerated unification.
scale: Information manipulation intentionally increased escalation risk.
column20: German History in Documents and Images — Ems Dispatch | Otto von Bismarck, Gedanken und Erinnerungen

title: Consolidating German unification as a federal empire
context: Victory over France opened the way for southern German states to join the northern federation.
decision: Supported a federal German Empire under Prussian kingship.
alternatives: Unitary state; loose confederation; postpone settlement.
rationale_reconstruction: Balance Prussian dominance with autonomy of German states.
criticism: The constitutional system concentrated substantial monarchical and military power.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — German Empire | German History in Documents and Images

title: Launching the Kulturkampf
context: Bismarck perceived the Catholic Church and Centre movement as competitors to state authority.
decision: Introduced measures restricting Catholic institutional influence.
alternatives: Tolerate opposition; negotiate with Centre; narrow measures.
rationale_reconstruction: Strengthen state authority and prevent an institution from organizing resistance.
outcome: Catholic institutions were restricted but the Centre Party remained resilient; policy was later moderated.
criticism: Coercion strengthened political resistance rather than eliminating it.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Kulturkampf | Jonathan Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life

title: Adopting Anti-Socialist Laws
context: After assassination attempts on Wilhelm I Bismarck framed socialist organization as a threat.
decision: Secured laws restricting socialist meetings organizations and publications.
alternatives: Legal competition; target only violent actors; broader compromise.
rationale_reconstruction: Contain an ideological movement through legal repression.
outcome: Socialist organization was constrained but survived and expanded electorally.
criticism: Coercion failed to eliminate the movement and damaged legitimacy.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Bismarck | German social policy histories

title: Hosting the Congress of Berlin
context: The Russo-Turkish War threatened a wider European crisis.
decision: Acted as broker to revise the settlement and contain great-power rivalry.
alternatives: Back one power; avoid mediation; allow bilateral settlement.
rationale_reconstruction: Prevent a Russo-British/Austrian confrontation and preserve Germany as broker.
outcome: Treaty of Berlin temporarily stabilized great-power relations.
criticism: Balkan tensions were postponed rather than resolved.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Congress of Berlin | Bismarck diplomatic history

title: Introducing compulsory health insurance
context: Industrialization and socialist growth created pressure for a new state-worker relationship.
alternatives: Pure repression; employer charity; liberal labor reform.
rationale_reconstruction: Use welfare provision to bind workers to the state and reduce socialist appeal.
outcome: Germany created pioneering national social insurance.
criticism: Policy had welfare effects but also regime-stabilization motives.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Bismarck | German social policy histories

title: Introducing accident insurance
context: Industrial accidents and labor unrest created demand for institutional responses.
alternatives: Private insurance; employer-only schemes; no national program.
rationale_reconstruction: Expand state capacity while managing industrial conflict.
outcome: Created another pillar of German social insurance.
criticism: Conservative political design limited worker control.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Bismarck | German social policy histories

title: Introducing old-age and disability insurance
context: Bismarck sought to integrate workers into the imperial state through social policy.
alternatives: Voluntary schemes; private pensions; broader democratic reform.
rationale_reconstruction: Create long-term state institutions and reduce socialist appeal.
outcome: Germany pioneered a modern social-insurance architecture.
criticism: Coverage and benefits were initially limited; motives were mixed.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Bismarck | German social policy histories

title: Securing the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia
context: Bismarck feared a two-front alignment of France and Russia.
decision: Negotiated secret neutrality with Russia while maintaining the Triple Alliance.
alternatives: Align exclusively with Austria; openly ally with Russia; accept drift.
rationale_reconstruction: Keep incompatible relationships manageable and prevent encirclement.
outcome: Germany temporarily balanced Russia and Austria.
criticism: System depended heavily on Bismarck personally and was hard to sustain after him.
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica — Bismarck | Bismarck diplomatic history

title: Losing office after conflict with Wilhelm II
context: Wilhelm II sought greater personal control and diverged from Bismarck's policies.
decision: Resisted the Kaiser's direction and ultimately left office.
rationale_reconstruction: Protect his policy system and authority while underestimating succession fragility.
outcome: Bismarck left office; German policy subsequently changed.
sources: Jonathan Steinberg, Bismarck: A Life | Encyclopaedia Britannica — Otto von Bismarck
